summary:
I've been building character-forge, a tool that turns an interview transcript into a full SillyTavern character card — lore, world membership, portraits, the works. The interesting problem is cache correctness: characters generated by an LLM tend to carry keyword-triggered lore entries, and every time a scene's wording shifts which entries fire, the prompt reshuffles and the model has to reprocess the whole conversation from scratch instead of reusing what it already computed. I traced a chain of "why is this slow" back to that, then found it was happening in two places at once — an embedded lore block inside the character file and a separate linked lorebook — and both had to be pinned to always-on before turns actually got fast again.

The harder bug was a silent data-loss case: rebuilding a character from its saved brief was supposed to reuse the interview transcript, but on a browser that never held that transcript, the build silently invented a new backstory and overwrote the real one. I patched it so a transcript-less rebuild works from the saved brief instead of inventing on an empty slate, and wrote a recovery path for the one character it happened to.

I also spent time on a subtler correctness rule: separating what belongs to a character card from what belongs to the person playing it. Early on, generated dialogue occasionally leaked assumptions about the player's gender or appearance from generated example lines. The fix was less about a code patch and more about drawing a clean boundary — a card should stay reusable across whoever plays it, and any player-specific detail belongs to a separate persona object, not baked into the character.

Alongside that I've kept tuning a small self-hosted model-serving layer that arbitrates a single shared GPU across a chat model, an image generator, and a couple of different LLM roles — worth mentioning mainly because "one GPU, several jobs that all want it now" turns out to be its own little scheduling problem, and getting eviction and warm-reload timing right cut a multi-second stall out of every cold request.

highlights.oneLiner: Tuned GPU broker sharing one P100 across chat, image gen, and LLM roles; fixed cold-start stalls
One of several LLM roles arbitrated behind the shared-GPU scheduling layer
Image generation leg competing for GPU time in the shared-model-serving setup
